title: The railway reaches Woking
text: The London and South Western Railway reaches Woking Common. Its fast main line out of London later makes a distant 'necropolis' practical: a train could carry the dead more quickly and cheaply than the horse-drawn hearses serving the existing cemeteries.

title: Cholera and overflowing graveyards
text: A cholera epidemic kills some 14,600–14,800 Londoners (sources give 14,601 and 14,789). The capital's churchyards and burial grounds, already notoriously overcrowded, cannot cope, and extramural burial becomes a matter of urgent public policy.

title: Broun and Sprye's great idea
text: Sir Richard Broun and Richard Sprye propose one vast cemetery on heathland at Brookwood, near Woking, served by its own trains from London. The site is about 23 miles from the capital, chosen because land there is cheap and the railway already runs past it.

title: Metropolitan Interments Act
text: Following the General Board of Health's report on extramural sepulture, the Metropolitan Interments Act creates a single Metropolitan Burial District under the Board, with power to close London's burial grounds and provide state cemeteries. The scheme proves too costly and is never effectively carried out.

title: The founders are bought out
text: Trustees led by William Voules buy the rights to the Brookwood scheme from Broun and Sprye for £20,000. They then form the company without regard to the original promoters, and Broun campaigns publicly against them.

title: The London Necropolis Act
text: The Act 'to incorporate the London Necropolis and National Mausoleum Company' (15 & 16 Vict. c. cxlix) receives Royal Assent, authorising a cemetery in the parish of Woking. Amending Acts follow in 1854, 1855 and 1864.

title: Burial Act repeals the state scheme
text: The Burial Act 1852 repeals the Metropolitan Interments Act. In its place it allows individual London burial grounds to be closed by Order in Council and sets up parish burial boards. The closures that follow create the market the Necropolis Company is counting on.

title: Land bought from Lord Onslow
text: Under the Act the company acquires Woking common land from Lord Onslow, given by Historic England as 2,268 acres; other accounts round it to about 2,000 acres. Only a few hundred acres at the western end are laid out as cemetery, and the rest becomes a land bank for later sales.

title: Crisis in the boardroom
text: Amid allegations of voting irregularities, and unable to pay the dividends it has promised, the company loses several directors, Voules among them, and public confidence collapses. The delays mean that by the time Brookwood opens, rival cemeteries nearer London are already open.

title: Sydney Smirke takes over
text: Sydney Smirke replaces the company's first architect, Henry Abraham, and designs the two cemetery chapels and stations. Smirke and William Broderick Thomas shape the landscape, which follows J. C. Loudon's principles, and the nurseryman Robert Donald of Goldsworth, Woking, carries out the planting.

title: Consecration
text: Charles Sumner, Bishop of Winchester, consecrates the southern, Church of England part of the cemetery, then called the Woking Necropolis, with its chapel. The northern part is left unconsecrated for Nonconformists and, later, other faiths.

title: First train, first burials
text: The first funeral train runs from the company's private station beside Waterloo, and the cemetery opens. The first interment is the stillborn twins of Mr and Mrs Hore of Ewer Street, Borough, buried at the expense of St Saviour's, Southwark; all that day's burials are pauper funerals in unmarked graves.

title: The first permanent memorial
text: Sir Henry Goldfinch dies. His memorial at Brookwood is identified as the first permanent memorial erected in the cemetery.

title: Actors' Acre
text: The actor John W. Anson acquires about an acre for the Dramatic, Equestrian and Musical Sick Fund Association as a burial place for actors and their families. Historic England dates the actors' ground to 1858.

title: Selling land: the invalid convict prison
text: Short of money, the company sells 64 acres of surplus land to the Government for the Woking Invalid Convict Prison. It is the first of many sales that fund the company and shape the district around it.

title: Friendly societies buy in
text: A plot is reserved for the Oddfellows' lodges of the Metropolitan District; its central memorial marks the plot's inauguration in October 1861. Guilds, trades and charities follow, including the Corps of Commissionaires and the Ancient Order of Foresters.

title: Zoroastrian burial ground opens
text: A burial ground for London's Parsi community opens in the north-west of the cemetery, a year after the community's religious trust fund was founded. It is described as the only Zoroastrian burial ground in Europe. One source dates the grant of burial rights to 1863.

title: A London graveyard moves to Surrey
text: Building Charing Cross station and its approaches requires clearing the Cure's College burial ground in Southwark, and some 7,950 bodies are taken to Brookwood. It is the first of many removals of London burial grounds to the cemetery.

title: Land for the county asylum
text: Some 150 acres of company land are bought for the second Surrey County Asylum at Brookwood, later Brookwood Hospital; a surveyor reports on the site in 1862. The asylum opens later in the decade.

title: The Royal Dramatic College
text: A college for retired actors opens at Maybury, Woking, on ten acres bought from the company for £750 (some sources date it to 1862). After it fails, its buildings pass by about 1883 to Dr Gottlieb Leitner's Oriental Institute, beside which the Shah Jahan Mosque rises in 1889.

title: Land for Britain's first crematorium
text: The Cremation Society buys about an acre at St John's, Woking, from the company, through a third party so that the cemetery company can keep its distance. One historian dates the purchase to 1874. The first cremation, of Jeannette Pickersgill, follows on 26 March 1885.

title: Britain's first Muslim burial ground
text: A small plot, 27 by 24 feet, is set aside for Leitner's Oriental Institute in Woking. Known as the 'Mohammedan Cemetery' and marked by a qibla stone, it is described as the first Muslim burial ground in Britain. Today Muslim burials account for more than 70 per cent of interments at Brookwood.

title: Chelsea Pensioners come to Brookwood
text: The Royal Hospital Chelsea, which had buried its in-pensioners at Brompton since 1855, begins using Brookwood; some accounts say 1894. A later pensioners' plot lies within Brookwood Military Cemetery.

title: No more Sunday trains
text: Sunday funeral trains end after October 1900. Trains had run once a day when funerals were booked; by the 1930s it was unusual for one to run more than twice a week.

title: A new London terminus
text: Needing the old site to enlarge Waterloo, the London and South Western Railway builds the company a new station at 121 Westminster Bridge Road, which Wikipedia dates to 8 February 1902. Its office frontage survives as Westminster Bridge House.

title: Jamsetji Tata buried at Brookwood
text: Jamsetji Nusserwanji Tata (1839–1904), founder of the Tata industrial empire, is buried in the Zoroastrian ground. The Tata mausolea join the earlier Wadia mausoleum, modelled on the tomb of Cyrus at Pasargadae.

title: Brookwood Military Cemetery
text: The company sets aside land for service men and women who die in the London area, the start of what is now Brookwood Military Cemetery, administered by the Commonwealth War Graves Commission. Burial figures and national plots should be confirmed with the CWGC.

title: A shorter name
text: The London Necropolis and National Mausoleum Company is renamed the London Necropolis Company.

title: The American cemetery dedicated
text: The Brookwood American Cemetery and Memorial, the only American First World War cemetery in Britain, is dedicated. It holds 468 American dead; another 564 missing, most of them lost at sea, are named on the walls of its chapel.

title: The last funeral train
text: The last funeral train leaves Westminster Bridge Road for Brookwood, reportedly carrying the Chelsea Pensioner Edward Irish (1868–1941).

title: The terminus is bombed
text: An air raid destroys the company's rolling stock and much of the London terminus. Only the platforms, the first-class waiting rooms and the office block survive. The station is formally closed on 11 May 1941.

title: The railway is given up
text: Having decided in September 1945 that the private train was obsolete, the company settles with the Southern Railway, and funerals use ordinary services from Waterloo to Brookwood instead. The track inside the cemetery is lifted around 1947–48.

title: The Brookwood 1939–1945 Memorial
text: Queen Elizabeth II unveils Ralph Hobday’s memorial to some 3,500 men and women of the Commonwealth land forces who died in the Second World War and have no known grave.

title: Horsell's Muslim soldiers moved
text: Because of vandalism, the Indian Army soldiers buried at the Muslim burial ground on Horsell Common near the Shah Jahan Mosque are moved to Brookwood Military Cemetery. The Horsell site became a Peace Garden in 2015.

title: A cemetery station is lost
text: One of Sydney Smirke's two cemetery stations is destroyed by vandals in 1972; the other had been demolished in the 1950s. Accounts generally identify the 1972 loss as the South station, whose platform survives.

title: End of the Necropolis Company
text: The London Necropolis Company is dissolved, and other private companies run the cemetery for a decade. The company's records were later saved from destruction by a former employee and are now at Surrey History Centre.

title: Orthodox monks arrive
text: Monks of the Russian Orthodox Church Outside Russia arrive to found the St Edward Brotherhood in the former Anglican chapels. In 1984 they enshrine the relics of St Edward the Martyr, the Anglo-Saxon king murdered in 978.

title: A private purchase
text: The cemetery is bought privately, by the Turkish Cypriot businessman Ramadan Güney according to most accounts. He was later buried there himself. It remains in private hands until Woking Borough Council acquires it.

title: Grade I landscape
text: Historic England registers Brookwood at Grade I on the Register of Parks and Gardens of Special Historic Interest, about 145 hectares, describing it as the largest cemetery in England. It is also on the Heritage at Risk register.

title: Death of Ramadan Güney
text: The cemetery’s owner since 1985 dies in Cyprus and is buried at Brookwood in one of the Muslim plots he helped to establish. His family continues to run the cemetery.

title: Woking Borough Council takes over
text: The council buys the companies that own the civilian cemetery, Brookwood Park Limited and Brookwood Cemetery Limited, on confidential terms. The war graves are not part of the sale.
